lesson_title: Halfway Up Two Rafters: the Midpoint Theorem
hook_text: The carpenter cuts the brace at the saw bench — before ever climbing. She already knows its length.
clip_script: A carport going up. Two rafters lean together at the ridge, and the base beam runs wall to wall — eight metres. The carpenter needs a cross-brace from rafter to rafter. So she marks halfway up the left rafter, halfway up the right, and fixes the brace between the marks. Two things happen, on every roof ever built this way. One: the brace sits dead level — exactly parallel to the beam below. Two: it measures exactly four metres. Half the beam. She could cut it at the saw bench before touching the ladder. That is the whole theorem: mark the middle of two sides of a triangle, join the marks, and the new piece is parallel to the third side and half its length. Beam twelve, brace six. Beam nine, brace four and a half. Why half? Cut along the brace, take the little top triangle, spin it a half-turn around the mark on the rafter — it clicks in beside the bottom piece and the two make a parallelogram. Two brace-lengths along the top, one beam along the bottom — and a parallelogram's top always equals its bottom. Two braces make one beam. The half was never a guess.
visual_style: A suburban carport frame at golden hour: rafters rising, chalk marks appearing at the halfway points, a brace clicking into place, then the top triangle rotating down to complete a glowing parallelogram.
pacing: Unhurried through the marking, a sharp beat on 'four metres', slow and deliberate on the spin.
